items.title: Metals get MORE resistive when heated; semiconductors get LESS
items.claim: Heat a copper wire and its resistance rises by about 0.4 percent per degree Celsius. Heat a semiconductor (like a thermistor) and its resistance falls dramatically. The two materials respond oppositely to temperature.
items.prompt: Why do metals and semiconductors behave oppositely?

options.text: In metals, increased temperature means more lattice vibrations (phonons) that scatter conduction electrons, raising resistance. In semiconductors, increased temperature liberates more charge carriers across the band gap, lowering resistance
The two have opposite signs of electric charge

items.reveal:
In a metal, the conduction electron density is essentially fixed (one or two per atom). Resistance is dominated by how often electrons scatter off lattice vibrations — more heat means more phonons, more scattering, more resistance. This is a positive temperature coefficient (PTC).

In an intrinsic semiconductor, conduction requires electrons (or holes) to be thermally excited across a band gap. The number of carriers rises exponentially with temperature (n ∝ exp(-Eg/2kT)). The carrier density swamps the scattering and resistance falls — a negative temperature coefficient (NTC).

NTC thermistors are used in temperature sensors (precision better than 0.1°C). PTC thermistors are used as self-resetting fuses — runaway heating raises their resistance and limits current.
items.why: Resistance is treated as a fixed property of a wire. It depends on which carriers are available — and that depends on temperature in very different ways for metals and semiconductors.

items.title: A pendulum trades potential and kinetic energy with no loss — in principle
items.claim: Pull a pendulum back to angle θ, release. At the bottom of the swing, all gravitational potential energy has become kinetic. Back at the top of the other side, all the kinetic energy is potential again. In an ideal frictionless pendulum, this swap continues forever.
items.prompt: Where does the energy actually go in a real pendulum?

options.text: It is destroyed at the bottom of the swing
Friction at the pivot, air resistance, and slight inelastic deformation of the string/rod all dissipate energy as heat. The amplitude decreases exponentially with each cycle (damped oscillation)
Energy is absorbed by Earth's gravitational field

items.reveal_title: Energy is conserved; the system simply transfers it out
items.reveal:
An ideal pendulum: m g L (1 - cos θ_max) of potential energy at the highest point becomes (1/2) m v² of kinetic energy at the bottom. The two trade places once per half-cycle.

A real pendulum loses some energy each cycle to friction at the pivot, drag through the air, and tiny inelastic effects in the string. The amplitude decays as exp(-t/τ) where τ is the time constant (typically minutes to hours for a good pendulum clock).

The pendulum's period for small angles is T = 2π√(L/g), independent of mass or amplitude. This is what made pendulum clocks accurate enough to be the global timekeeping standard from 1656 (Huygens) until ~1929 (when quartz oscillators overtook them).
items.why: Conservation of energy is taught as a static law. In a real oscillator it constrains where the energy goes — but it doesn't keep it all where you want it.
